title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description: Maximum profit obtainable from buying once and selling once on later days.
statement:
You are given a daily price series `prices` for a single instrument.

You may perform **at most one** transaction: pick a day to buy and a strictly later day to sell. The profit is `prices[sell] - prices[buy]`.

Report the largest profit available. If no transaction can be profitable - the series is empty, has a single day, or only ever falls - report `0`, which stands for choosing not to trade at all.

Scanning the series once while remembering the cheapest price seen so far is enough; a full search over all buy/sell pairs is unnecessary.
inputFormat:
The input is read from standard input as exactly two lines:

1. Line 1: integer `n` - the number of prices (`0 <= n <= 100000`).
2. Line 2: `n` space-separated integers `prices[0] ... prices[n-1]`. When `n` is 0 this line is empty.
outputFormat: Print a single line containing the maximum achievable profit as a single integer (`0` when no profitable transaction exists).
constraints: The buy day must come strictly before the sell day
The answer fits in a signed 64-bit integer
notes: `n = 0` is legal and the answer is `0`. Prices may be negative, which changes nothing: only the difference between two days matters. Buying and selling on the same day yields `0`, so it can never beat a real profit and never needs to be considered separately.

Step 2: at 1 the minimum drops to 1, so any later sale is measured from 1.
Step 3: selling at 5 gives 5-1=4, at 6 gives 5, at 4 gives 3.
Step 4: the best sale is 6 minus the minimum 1, so the answer is 5.

Step 2: buying at any earlier day always costs more than selling on a later day.
Step 3: no single transaction can earn a positive profit.
Step 4: the best achievable profit is therefore 0.
